visual.title: Three levels of medication reasoning, kept apart
visual.description: A labeled separation of drug action, typical burden, and individual experience, so general knowledge is not mistaken for personal advice.
steps: Action: what the medicine does pharmacologically, which is comparatively well characterised
Burden: the pattern of effects across many users, which justifies monitoring
Person: what this individual experiences, which requires clinical review to assess
Conversation: the question to ask a prescriber, containing no dose or change of its own

lessons.title: Psychotherapy modalities and the evidence that supports them
lessons.explanation: The objective is to understand that psychological therapies are not interchangeable, and that evidence supports particular approaches for particular difficulties. Cognitive behavioural therapy examines relationships among thoughts, feelings, and behaviour and typically involves practice between sessions. Behaviour therapy uses graded exposure to reduce avoidance. Behavioural activation focuses on activity, avoidance, and opportunities for reward. Interpersonal therapy addresses problems in relationships and how they are handled. Counselling offers a space to talk through thoughts, feelings, and experiences. Guided self-help delivers structured material, usually based on cognitive behavioural principles, with therapist support.[1] Across these, the common thread is a structured relationship with a rationale, not a single technique. NICE recommends specific psychological approaches for specific conditions, and Royal College of Psychiatrists material sets out which approaches address which problems.[2] This lesson explains how to read that evidence; it does not recommend a therapy for any individual.
lessons.example: A fictional person describes repeated checking and seeks a talking therapy because they have heard that counselling helps with anxiety. A useful comparison asks what each option targets. A structured approach built on exposure addresses the avoidance and ritual cycle directly. A general counselling conversation may help the person feel heard and understood, which matters, but is not designed around the specific maintaining process. Neither is inherently superior as an experience; they differ in what they aim to change and in what the evidence supports for this particular difficulty. The recommended reasoning is therefore not 'therapy is good' but 'which approach, targeting which process, for which problem, with what evidence'. Royal College material organises exactly this way, setting out the approach alongside the problems it is used for.[2]
lessons.question: A service offers the same therapy to everyone on the grounds that 'talking therapy works'. What is the main reasoning error?
lessons.answer: Evidence supports specific approaches for specific difficulties, so the claim generalises across indications and modalities
lessons.distractor: Talking therapies have no evidence and should not be offered
lessons.correction: The error is over-generalisation, not the existence of evidence. Many psychological approaches have good evidence for particular problems and much weaker evidence for others.

depth.definitions: Psychotherapy is a structured psychological treatment delivered through a relationship, with a rationale and a defined focus. Cognitive behavioural therapy targets the interaction of thoughts, feelings, and behaviour, with between-session practice. Exposure is a controlled, planned approach to a feared situation or memory, delivered in a graded way. Behavioural activation schedules activity that is meaningful or rewarding and examines the function of avoidance. Interpersonal therapy focuses on relationship difficulties and the transitions and disputes that shape them. Psychodynamic approaches examine patterns that recur across relationships and their origins. Guided self-help is structured material with support. Common factors are the elements shared across therapies, such as a therapeutic alliance and a coherent rationale, and they are distinct from the specific techniques a modality adds.
depth.mechanism: Testing psychological treatments is methodologically demanding, because neither the person nor the therapist can be blinded to which therapy is being delivered, and because the therapist's skill and the quality of delivery vary. Evidence therefore needs to be read with attention to what was compared, in whom, on which outcome, and over what follow-up, just as with any other treatment evidence. The practical consequence is that 'evidence-based therapy' is a statement about a specific pairing of approach and problem rather than a general blessing. NICE's depression guidance recommends specific structured approaches and discusses their delivery demands,[3] reflecting the same specificity. A further subtlety is that many therapies share common factors, so some of the benefit may come from elements that are not unique to any modality. This does not make the differences unimportant; it makes attributing benefit to a named technique more difficult than it first appears.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the checking case with a fictional person whose main difficulty is a pervasive sense of hopelessness and withdrawal from previously valued activities. Here an approach built around reactivating activity and examining the function of avoidance addresses a different maintaining process, and the questions that matter concern what the person has stopped doing and why. Now imagine a clinic that swaps the two plans. Both therapies are legitimate and evidence-supported in their own place; the mismatch is with the maintaining process, not with the modality's quality. This is why assessment comes before approach, and why a formulation that identifies what keeps a difficulty going is the bridge between them. The same logic explains why the modality label alone tells you little about whether the treatment will suit this person.
depth.mistake: The most common error is treating talking therapies as interchangeable, so that availability rather than fit determines what is offered. A second is assuming that popularity or public familiarity is evidence; a widely known approach may have strong evidence for one problem and weak evidence for another. A third is dismissing a therapy because it did not work once, without asking whether it was delivered as intended, whether the agreed tasks were feasible, or whether the difficulty was one the approach targets. Correct these by naming the specific approach and the specific problem together, checking that delivery matched the intended model, and reviewing outcomes against the person's own goals rather than against a general impression of improvement.
depth.application: Practice without any personal information. For three fictional difficulties, note a psychological approach whose rationale matches the maintaining process and one sentence explaining the match: repeated checking with a feared consequence; withdrawal and loss of rewarding activity; intrusive memories after a traumatic event. A model response pairs a structured exposure-based approach with the checking cycle, behavioural activation with withdrawal and lost reward, and a trauma-focused approach with intrusive memories, noting in each case which process the approach targets. Self-review: each pairing names both the approach and the process, you have not claimed that one modality is best overall, and you have stated what would count as evidence that the match was wrong. This is an academic exercise, not a treatment recommendation.
depth.summary: Psychological therapies are structured, specific, and unevenly evidenced across problems. The useful question is never whether therapy works in general but which approach targets which maintaining process with what evidence for this kind of difficulty. Read alongside the previous lesson, this closes the loop on treatment reasoning: medicines and psychological approaches both act on processes, both carry characteristic burdens, and neither substitutes for a formulation that identifies what is actually being addressed.

visual.title: Matching an approach to a maintaining process
visual.description: A labeled sequence showing why the modality label alone does not determine fit.
steps: Identify the maintaining process from the formulation
Name the specific approach designed to target that process
State what the evidence supports for this problem, in this population, on which outcome
Review the match against the person's own goals and revise if it did not fit

questions.prompt: A person is described as having recurrent depression. The history includes a period of several days with almost no need for sleep, unusual confidence, and greatly increased activity. What does this change?
questions.answer: A past elevated episode with increased energy alters which mood syndrome family is under consideration
questions.distractor: It shows only that the current depressive episode is more severe than earlier ones
questions.correction: Severity and category are separate questions. The presence of a past elevated episode with increased activity is what distinguishes bipolar from unipolar patterns.

questions.prompt: Two people describe hearing voices. One has had the experience for three days after a bereavement and retains insight; the other for eight months with declining function and loss of insight. What separates the reasoning?
questions.answer: Duration, course, insight, distress, and functional change, considered together
questions.distractor: Whether the voices are experienced as coming from inside or outside the head
questions.correction: Duration, course, insight, distress, and functional change are what separate candidate categories in this family. Whether a voice seems to come from inside or outside the head is a descriptive detail worth noting, but it does not settle the category on its own.

questions.prompt: A person repeatedly checks locks and asks others for reassurance. What single question best distinguishes an anxiety pattern from an obsessive-compulsive pattern?
questions.answer: Whether an unwanted intrusive thought precedes the checking and is briefly neutralised by it
questions.distractor: Whether the person feels anxious while checking the locks
questions.correction: Anxiety is reported in both. The distinguishing structure is the intrusive thought and the neutralising ritual, which changes what maintains the cycle.

questions.prompt: A person asks why two medicines for the same problem produce such different side effects. Which explanation is most honest?
questions.answer: The classes act differently and therefore tend to produce different kinds of burden, though individual experience varies
questions.distractor: One class corrects a chemical deficiency and the other does not
questions.correction: The classes have different pharmacological actions and characteristic profiles, but the deficiency framing overstates what is known and does not account for individual variation.

questions.prompt: A clinic offers one psychological therapy to everyone because 'talking therapy works'. What is the reasoning error, and what would correct it?
questions.answer: It generalises across indications and modalities; the correction is to name the approach and the specific difficulty together
questions.distractor: It assumes evidence exists where none does for any talking therapy
questions.correction: The problem is over-generalisation rather than an absence of evidence. Many approaches have good evidence for particular difficulties and much weaker evidence for others.

questions.prompt: A person reports low mood, and an examiner notes reduced movement and a change in weight. A colleague writes 'endogenous depression' in the record on that basis. Using the levels of description and the structure of criteria sets, what is the strongest correction?
questions.answer: Symptoms and signs have been observed; whether a category applies still depends on duration, impact, exclusion rules, and a criteria set
questions.distractor: The term is acceptable because observable signs carry more weight than reported symptoms
questions.correction: Signs and symptoms are data; a category is a rule-governed conclusion. Nothing about observing signs removes the need to check the criteria components, including duration and exclusions.

questions.prompt: A record states that a person was 'uncooperative, thought-disordered, and hostile'. The examiner's setting was a noisy corridor and questions were put rapidly in the person's second language. What combination best repairs the record?
questions.answer: Rewrite it as observable description, reported content, and recorded context, and mark any remaining interpretation as a hypothesis
questions.distractor: Retain the terms but add that the person was difficult to interview
questions.correction: The terms compress observation and inference and omit the conditions that produced the behaviour. Separating observation, report, context, and inference makes the record checkable and revisable.

questions.prompt: A twenty-year-old describes eight months of withdrawal and unusual beliefs with slow onset and steady decline. A sixty-eight-year-old describes two days of talkativeness and agitation. A service applies the same assessment pathway to both. What is wrong with that reasoning?
questions.answer: Tempo and age of onset shift the ranking of explanations, so the two presentations warrant different priorities rather than one shared pathway
questions.distractor: Nothing, because the same criteria set can be applied to any age group
questions.correction: The same category structure can apply across ages, but the differential and its urgency depend heavily on acuity and age of onset. One pathway ignores that difference.

questions.prompt: A person meeting full criteria for a depressive category has no history of elevated mood; another with the same current features has one clear past episode of decreased sleep need and increased activity. Both records say 'depression'. What does the comparison illustrate about criteria and course?
questions.answer: Meeting a criteria set describes the present pattern, while past episodes can change which syndrome family is relevant even when the current features match
questions.distractor: The second person's record is correct because depression always precedes elevated episodes
questions.correction: The point is not automatic precedence but the informational value of a rare past episode. Course is part of the reasoning and is lost when only the current episode is recorded.

questions.prompt: A person checks the door a dozen times. In one account they fear a vague sense of dread; in another an unwanted image of harm intrudes and the checking briefly silences it. A service writes 'anxiety, offer general reassurance'. What correction follows?
questions.answer: The two accounts suggest different maintaining processes, and reassurance may sustain rather than resolve the second pattern
questions.distractor: Reassurance is always the safest first step because it reduces distress immediately
questions.correction: Immediate relief is not the same as resolution. Where a ritual neutralises an intrusion, repeated reassurance can form part of the cycle, so the process must be identified before the response.

questions.prompt: A person is seen after a single brief episode of hearing voices that resolved within a week, and separately after eight months of unusual beliefs with loss of insight and declining function. A trainee calls both 'psychosis, so same risk, same plan'. What is the error?
questions.answer: Duration and course separate the candidate categories, and the risk question requires its own assessment rather than an inference from a label
questions.distractor: Both should be treated identically because the experiences are of the same kind
questions.correction: The category question turns on duration and course, and equating a category with dangerousness is a separate and damaging error. Each requires individual assessment.

questions.prompt: A person reports that a medicine improved their mood but left them unable to study. A relative says the medicine 'fixed the chemical imbalance' and that the tiredness proves the person is not trying. What reasoning should replace this?
questions.answer: Separate the drug's pharmacological action from the unexplained cause of the difficulty, and separate the class burden from this person's experience
questions.distractor: Accept that a favourable mood response identifies both the cause and the correct medicine
questions.correction: Drug action, typical class burden, and individual experience are three different claims. None of them identifies the origin of the difficulty, and none justifies attributing a new symptom to effort.

questions.prompt: A service concludes that psychological therapy is 'proven', then offers the same approach to everyone. A person with intrusive memories after a traumatic event receives a general counselling conversation and does not improve. What conclusions are warranted?
questions.answer: The approach was not matched to the maintaining process, and evidence supports specific approaches for specific difficulties rather than one blanket claim
questions.distractor: The therapy failed, so psychological therapy is ineffective for this kind of difficulty
questions.correction: One delivery of a mismatched approach does not evaluate a modality. The relevant questions are which process was targeted, whether the approach was delivered as intended, and what the evidence supports for this specific difficulty.

questions.prompt: A person with a long-standing psychiatric diagnosis becomes newly withdrawn and sleepy over two days. The note reads that the diagnosis explains the change and no further assessment is needed. Which two reasoning failures are combined here?
questions.answer: Diagnostic overshadowing and premature closure, both corrected by re-ranking the differential on tempo and consequence
questions.distractor: Over-investigation and unnecessary escalation of a stable presentation
questions.correction: A familiar label does not explain a new abrupt change, and settling on the first explanation stops the reasoning. Acute tempo and the consequence of missing a medical contributor should re-rank the differential.

questions.prompt: Two clinicians argue. One says the manual defines the disorder, so disagreement is impossible. The other says categories are conventional, so they are worthless. Using the examination record, the criteria structure, and the evidence base for therapy, what is the defensible position?
questions.answer: Categories are operational conventions valuable for communication and research, and they are useful precisely when their evidence, limits, and reliability are stated
questions.distractor: Agreement between clinicians proves the category corresponds to a distinct underlying process
questions.correction: Reliability is not validity. Categories remain indispensable for shared language while their thresholds and heterogeneity stay open to challenge, and the same discipline applies to records and to treatment evidence.

questions.prompt: A service plans one pathway for a young person with gradual withdrawal and unusual beliefs, an older adult with two days of agitation, and a person with post-traumatic intrusions, on the grounds that all three involve 'altered mental state'. What is missing?
questions.answer: Tempo, age of onset, and the different maintaining processes of the three presentations, each of which changes priority and approach
questions.distractor: Nothing, provided the same criteria set is applied to all three
questions.correction: The three presentations differ in urgency, in the medical contributors that must be ranked, and in the processes that maintain them. A shared label does not create a shared pathway.

questions.prompt: A learner writes that a category 'is caused by low serotonin, is confirmed when an SSRI helps, and is treated with the same therapy for everyone'. Identify the reasoning in each clause and the correct position.
questions.answer: Each clause converts a convention, an outcome, or a general finding into a certainty that the evidence does not support
questions.distractor: The statement is acceptable because each clause reflects a published source
questions.correction: Criteria do not identify causes, response is not a diagnostic test, and psychological treatments are evidence-based for specific difficulties. Sources support claims at the level they were made.
